arXiv:2610.37739v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in research-level problem solving, yet a comprehensive collection of such problems is still missing, and evaluating them on research-level problems remains challenging. We introduce OpenFrontiers, a cross-disciplinary resource that combines a structured corpus of open research problems with a retrospective benchmark of recently resolved problems in mathematics. The corpus records problem statements, context, progress, and other information for 12,151 problems. The benchmark contains 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, each with a Lean~4 statement checked by automated probes and two independent reviews; a subset HQ-50 further filters based on quality score, etc. Our evaluation protocol grades formal proofs with two independent checkers in an isolated sandbox under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions. Evaluating seven LLM agents on the HQ-50 subset under a standardized budget, we find that closed-book rediscovery is rare, at most 7 of 40 resolved problems, whereas live-web success mostly reflects retrieval of published solutions. By linking a broad research-problem corpus to a formally graded evaluation subset with documented solutions, OpenFrontiers provides a foundation for measuring research-level rediscovery and studying progress toward solving currently open scientific problems. The dataset and benchmark could be found in https://huggingface.co/collections/FlippyDora/openfrontiers.
title: OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery

arXiv:2610.37809v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents that answer questions over Web knowledge graphs are increasingly wrapped in checks derived from the graph's ontology, on the assumption that a formal schema makes a reliable judge. Yet a checker can be wrong as well: it can miss errors, and it can flag correct answers and push the agent into "fixing" them. Whether a curated ontology is worth its cost as such a judge, and how it compares with an ontology an LLM writes or a schema mined from the data, is unknown. We make the checker itself the object of study. Across curated, LLM-generated and data-derived ontologies, used as prompt context, as a checker, or both, and across open-weight and proprietary agents on public graphs and a private graph of nearly $10^{9}$ triples, we account for what ontology-derived checks catch and what they wrongly flag. We show how each source trades caught errors against false alarms, how a curated schema used as published can contradict its own data, which errors structural checks miss, and whether combining sources or giving the agent the checker's specific feedback pays off. On UniProt, the curated ontology flags more correct answers than either an ontology derived from the data or one an LLM derives from a summary of the data with masked identifiers. On real agent answers, its flags are only marginally more precise than random flags.
title: What Does an Ontology Catch? Curated, LLM-Generated and Data-Derived Ontologies as Checkers of LLM Agents over Knowledge Graphs

arXiv:2610.37830v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents can now write software from a plain-English description, but code that runs is not the same as code that does what was asked. This gap matters most for smart contracts, the programs behind Web3 applications that move money on a blockchain and cannot be fixed once deployed. We ask how to check whether an AI-written contract behaves as it should, and where the requested behavior gets lost.
  We design an evaluation built on execution rather than opinion. We replay the same transactions on an AI-written contract and on the original it should reproduce and measure how often they agree. We test every grading tool on planted mistakes, compare against an answer key written without the description, and audit our own scorer until known wrong answers cannot pass. Common methods, such as AI judges and standard analysis tools, miss obvious mistakes, and scoring choices matter too. Checking only the functions every system includes hid about half the difference between pipelines.
  We then propose an elicitation-first architecture. Before writing code, the agent asks the client a short checklist of questions, checks the contract against an independently written executable answer key, and returns disagreements to the client instead of silently rewriting code. Asking first matters far more than reviewing or patching afterwards, across three AI models, while automated security fixes often break requested behavior. A few well-chosen questions recover much of what a short description omits, and their value can be estimated without the original contract. To our knowledge, this is the first study in smart contract synthesis to gather missing requirements before generation and check the result against an independently written executable model. The lessons extend to any setting where AI agents turn requests into programs. We release our tools, 600 tasks and all results.
title: Measuring Where Intent Gets Lost in Agentic Smart Contract Synthesis

Let’s dive in!

Product, technology, and tools updates

  • New compute service: Agent Compute Engine is a purpose-built compute service providing high-performance, hardware-isolated microVM sandboxes alongside expanded agent governance capabilities like Agent Gateway and Agent Registry, all in the service of securing and scaling autonomous AI agents. Its primary benefits include rapid sub-second activation, extreme workload density through copy-on-write memory sharing, enterprise-grade security and identity management, and cross-cloud observability.

These co-engineered advancements provide enterprises with accelerated performance, enhanced sovereign AI controls, while advanced Confidential Computing capabilities help you train and deploy complex multi-step models securely and efficiently.

  • GKE product update: CPU startup boost for GKE, in preview, uses Kubernetes In-place Pod Resize to dynamically elevate container CPU resources during initialization and scale them back down to steady-state levels without having to restart the containers. This feature removes startup throttling and accelerates cold starts by up to 2x for demanding workloads, helping to lower cloud infrastructure costs.

  • GKE product update: The preview of the Wiz Runtime Sensor add-on for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) brings low-touch deployment, automated lifecycle management, enterprise credential security, and fleet-wide governance to Wiz's eBPF runtime threat detection for both Standard and Autopilot GKE clusters.

Enterprise teams now have purpose-built agentic capabilities across infrastructure assessment, platform modernization, and application modernization.

This integration eliminates cluster management, lowers costs, using Temporal Worker Versioning to safely handle stateful, long-running workflows and AI agent workloads.

Abstract: Web agents require diverse, executable, and resettable website environments for reproducible training and evaluation. Human-assisted mirrors demand per-site engineering, while generative construction can diverge from specified real websites. raw_summary:
arXiv:2610.37849v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents that share a secret convention can coordinate through messages that look innocent, so a monitor that reads only the messages can miss them. We propose a behavioural test: a partner that uses a code reacts to the exact wording of a message, whereas an uninvolved agent placed in its seat does not. Partner--Outsider Positive Listening (PoPLi) is the difference between the two agents in how much their action changes when the message is reworded with its meaning kept, and it is computed after the fact by replaying logged prompts. In a simulated market with five conditions (no collusion, a joint reward with neutral messages, the same with an openly stated intention, a covert first-letter code, and the code with a stated intention), PoPLi is between 0.48 and 0.59 whenever the code is present (95% intervals all above 0.29) and between -0.10 and -0.01 without it. Message-only monitors did not separate the conditions: one reading the speaker's messages answered "no" in all 50 markets, and one reading every seller's messages flagged 9 of 10 markets with no collusion. PoPLi detects the use of a private channel, not collusion as such, and it cannot detect collusion through incentives alone or codes carried by meaning.
title: Detecting Covert Collusion between AI Agents through Partner-Outsider Positive Listening

arXiv:2610.37851v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing scientific-agent benchmarks rarely evaluate whether agents can reconstruct the exact molecular structures and generation workflows specified by sequencing protocols, a capability critical for analyzing customized sequencing assays. We introduce LibStructBench, a document-grounded benchmark for reconstructing sequencing-library structures and molecular workflows. Our experiments show that frontier agents often produce approximately correct reconstructions but remain unreliable at exact reconstruction, particularly in molecular-state representation and workflow connectivity. Switching the underlying language model produced larger average performance differences than switching agent harnesses, with a statistically significant difference only for molecular-state reconstruction. Additional knowledge improved oligo-family recovery in a small pilot without improving mean molecular-workflow scores. Autonomous accumulation of procedural rules and cross-protocol examples showed non-monotonic validation performance and no mean held-out molecular-workflow improvement in the tested trajectory. These findings highlight the need for more controlled and verifiable approaches to scientific reasoning about molecular processes in complex experimental protocols.
title: Evaluating and improving AI agents for sequencing protocol understanding

Teams created on or after October 30, 2026 use Runtime Cache by default.

raw_summary:
Today, we’re bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache, giving developers one product for data caching across frameworks and APIs. If you use Next.js fetch caching or unstable_cache, you won’t need to change your code. Pro and Enterprise projects will get larger storage allocations.

Runtime Cache lets your code reuse fetched or computed data across requests without operating a separate caching service. Over the past year, we’ve improved read performance during traffic bursts, increased storage budgets, and made cache usage easier to investigate.

Why we built Runtime Cache

Data Cache was originally launched as Vercel’s data caching service for the Next.js App Router, used by fetch caching and unstable_cache. Unlike CDN caching, which stores complete HTTP responses, Data Cache stores data your application uses to generate those responses. A product page, for example, can reuse cached catalog data while rendering a personalized response for each visitor.

We wanted developers to have access to that service without depending on Next.js. Last year, we introduced Runtime Cache with a direct API: getCache from @vercel/functions. Applications can use it for feature flag lookups in Routing Middleware, caching CMS content during builds, and data caching in SvelteKit and Nuxt apps.

Frameworks can expose this service through their own APIs, too. On Vercel, Next.js itself uses the Runtime Cache API for 'use cache: remote', which caches function and component outputs.

How Runtime Cache works

The infrastructure behind Runtime Cache is a distributed caching service shared by many teams. A Go API handles requests, backed by Redis fleets in every Vercel region. Every hour, the service handles more than 440 million reads and moves more than 18 TB of data.

Each region has its own cache. A cache hit takes one round trip to the cache service in the region where your code runs. Vercel handles authentication with short-lived credentials, so you don’t need to manage API keys.

On a cache miss, your app or framework fetches or computes the value and writes it to that region’s cache. The service doesn’t check other regions for a cached copy.

Each cached entry stores its tags and write time. When the service reads an entry, it checks a separate tag store in the same region for those tags’ invalidation timestamps. If any tag was invalidated after the entry was written, the entry is stale.

For example, an application can tag all its cached product data with catalog. When the catalog changes, invalidating that tag writes a single timestamp, even if a million entries share the tag. The service doesn’t need to find and delete those entries individually.

The invalidation immediately updates the tag store in the region receiving the request. Vercel’s shared tag infrastructure, also used by the CDN, distributes the timestamp through the global push pipeline, typically reaching other regions within a few hundred milliseconds.

Your app or framework chooses what to cache and handles misses. Runtime Cache handles regional storage, authentication, and distributing tag invalidations across regions.

What we’ve shipped

Faster reads during traffic bursts

Checking whether an entry is still fresh adds a dependency to every cache hit. During traffic bursts, a slow shard in the tag store could delay reads even when the cached value was already available.

We added circuit breakers that let reads temporarily check freshness using tag timestamps cached in memory, so they can proceed without waiting for the slow shard to respond. During this fallback, a read can briefly treat recently invalidated data as fresh.

We enabled the breakers in every region in August. During the heaviest bursts in our largest region, p99 cache-service read latency fell to about one fifth of its previous level at comparable traffic. On-call alerts for this failure mode stopped.

More storage and fewer evictions

We raised Runtime Cache storage budgets for Pro projects in June and Enterprise projects in October, giving applications more room for data they reuse. This reduces the need to evict cached entries to make room for new data. Among Enterprise projects with frequent evictions, cache miss rates roughly halved within a day.

More visibility into cache behavior

We’ve added deployment markers, revalidation causes, and write utilization to the Runtime Cache view in Observability. These help you compare changes in cache behavior with releases, see why entries are refreshed, and identify data that gets written to the cache but rarely read.

Bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache

We’re simplifying caching on Vercel by consolidating on Runtime Cache. Until now, Next.js fetch caching and unstable_cache have used Data Cache, while getCache and 'use cache: remote' have used Runtime Cache. The migration brings all four APIs under Runtime Cache, so you and coding agents have one set of storage budgets and usage tools to work with.

If you use fetch caching or unstable_cache, nothing changes in your code. On Pro, each project and environment gets its own storage allocation, with 8x the space of Data Cache’s previous team-wide pool. Enterprise projects get 10x their previous Data Cache storage.

Previously unbilled Data Cache reads and writes will follow Runtime Cache pricing. New teams use Runtime Cache automatically, and existing teams will receive their migration and billing details in advance.

See the changelog for the rollout, pricing, and early opt-in details. Before migrating, review your cache usage and follow the optimization guide to reduce unnecessary reads and writes.

Today, we’re announcing that spend caps on Google Cloud Budgets are generally available. 

With this release, we’re delivering ways to protect your workloads from runaway costs without risking resource deletion. More importantly, we’re introducing three major updates, directly inspired by your feedback since the initial preview, to bring programmability, real-time visibility, and automated guardrails to your cost-control playbook.

How the new spend caps can help your business 

We have significantly enhanced the usability and power of spend caps in three ways: 

1. Automation through spend caps API: Managing guardrails manually across hundreds of projects is a major operational challenge. To address this, we have launched the spend caps API, which can be accessed from the existing Cloud Billing Budgets API. You can now programmatically enforce your financial boundaries for eligible services within each project, without additional overhead. You can automatically lift, update, or delete caps on the fly and instantly apply a spend cap whenever a developer spins up a new sandbox project.

2. Real-time visibility with live cost reports: Spend caps for AI services trigger within minutes of usage using estimated, live costs. When a cap triggers, you need to know exactly why and when the limit was breached. You can now view these faster, estimated costs directly inside your Cost Reports. Instead of waiting hours for standard billing pipelines to settle net costs, you get the exact financial snapshots that triggered the enforcement, giving you the immediate context needed to run a precise root-cause analysis.

3. Automated guardrails for your monthly resets: Before, once a spend cap was triggered, the usage block remained locked until you manually lifted it in the UI. Today, we are introducing automated monthly resets. You no longer need to worry about manually lifting caps every month. Enforced spend caps will automatically reset, and blocked services will seamlessly resume at the beginning of the next month. However, if your governance policies require a strict manual audit before resuming operations, the manual override option continues to exist exactly as before. 

Best practices for deploying spend caps

As you roll out spend caps across your organization, keep these operational tips in mind:

  1. Target non-production environments first: Start by applying strict, low-dollar spend caps to your developer sandboxes, testing clusters, and experimental AI agent playgrounds.
  2. Configure alerts wisely: Default alerts are automatically sent to billing administrators and project owners at 50%, 80%, and 100% of the cap. Make sure the right folks are set up in these roles. This ensures your team is never caught off guard when a budget is nearing depletion. Spend caps permissions can also be added to custom roles, if needed.  
  3. Understand fixed vs on-demand costs: Spend caps halt pay-as-you-go and CUD-covered requests once the budget threshold is hit. However, Provisioned Throughput is never halted; requests using reserved capacity will continue to run, and serve traffic normally.

Refresher on GCP’s dual-pronged defense playbook

Spend Caps work seamlessly alongside our native Early Anomalies Detection to provide a closed-loop defense for your cloud spend. Read our previous blog for a detailed explanation on how to use these tools to effortlessly set up a GCP defense playbook.

raw_summary:
Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. From there it grew into Geist Sans for product interfaces, and then into Geist Pixel, which was inspired by the grids of early computer screens.

Today, we're adding a new member to the family: Geist Serif.

Geist Serif is a high-contrast display serif built on the same foundations as Geist Sans, Geist Mono, and Geist Pixel. It has fine, saw-toothed serifs and sharp hairlines, and it was drawn to communicate messages powerfully both in the physical world and on the high-density screens on modern devices.

Same system, new voice

At Vercel, Geist Sans runs the product. For headlines, though, we wanted a second voice, one that belongs to the same system, instead of a stranger picked from a drop-down menu.

A lot of tech brands have moved away from clean sans-serifs to get some personality back, and many of them borrow from vintage computer ads. Geist Serif takes a different path: toward fashion, editorial design, and magazine headlines. It's our homage to the artists behind Rolling Stone and Harper's Bazaar.

From the beginning, each Geist family has read from a chapter of type history: the Swiss design movement, early terminal and DOS computing, and now editorial print.

Display first

Geist Serif began as a set of sketches by Evil Rabbit, which Andrés Briganti then expanded. The first letters already showed an expressive serif, in the spirit of typefaces like Victor Serif and Stanley.

When Mark Davis took over the drawings, we made the first release a display face for headlines, posters, and other large sizes, while work on the full family continued. Print has always struggled to hold fine hairlines and sharp serifs, but today's displays can handle a high level of detail. We wanted the new face to take full advantage of modern screens, so we thinned every downstroke by 50% and tightened the sidebearings to push the contrast as far as it would go.

Each serif has a wedge on one side and a curve on the other, so the proportions are classical and look beautiful in print, but the construction is new and optimized for digital devices.

From the first prototype to today

The first prototype of Geist Serif was shared on April 1, 2026. Here's the same word, Geist, in that prototype, compared with the display drawing shipping today.

Geist grew teeth

The goal was to honor our original intent and keep the serif closely tied to the sans, even when the letters sit on top of each other. Geist Serif’s stems match Geist Sans, and the two share widths and postures.

The saw-toothed serifs and high contrast give Geist an editorial voice. One phrase kept coming up as each character was drawn: “Geist grew teeth.”

Four families, one x-height

Geist Serif uses the same cap height and x-height as Geist Sans, so you can drop it into any Geist layout without moving a line. Mix Sans, Mono, Pixel, and Serif in the same sentence and every word looks the same size.

Four variants, one axis

Like Geist Pixel, Geist Serif has a variable axis that swaps the shape of every dot in the font, including those on i and j and in punctuation. The axis is called Element Shape (ELSH), and it gives you four variants: Regular with round dots (the default), Square, Triangle (a nod to the Vercel logo), and Heart.

Each variant also ships as its own static file. If you use the variable font, pick a variant with font-variation-settings:

Crafted by hand

In July the font had 227 glyphs. It now has 894 and covers 352 Latin-script languages, and we worked through more than 52,000 kerning pairs to get the spacing right. Some of the details are tiny. The eye of the g, for example, is tilted exactly 7°.

  • 1 weight (Regular)

  • 4 variants (Regular, Square, Triangle, Heart)

  • 894 glyphs

  • 5 stylistic sets (ss01 to ss05)

  • 352 supported languages

  • GeistSerif (variable, all shapes): --font-geist-serif

  • GeistSerifRegular: --font-geist-serif-regular

  • GeistSerifSquare: --font-geist-serif-square

  • GeistSerifTriangle: --font-geist-serif-triangle

  • GeistSerifHeart: --font-geist-serif-heart

Each one has its own entry point, so you only ship the font file you use. For example, in layout.tsx with GeistSerifRegular:

You can also download the font files, test every stylistic set, and inspect each glyph at vercel.com/font.

What’s next

Regular is the first style we’re releasing, and the rest of the family is already in progress. We’re testing future versions while building this one, so this release is just the start.

Weights from Thin to Black

The variable font will range from Thin (100) to Black (900). In this week’s proofs, the g in Black is the letter we can’t stop looking at.

Toward a text face

To explore a text version, we built a foundry tool that measures strokes, including where they meet, and thickens the display outlines. It edits the outlines directly, so we can set real words and see which strokes need more weight.

Italics, built rule by rule

We’re also developing an italic generated entirely in Python. We slanted existing italics back upright and compared them with their romans. With the angle removed, the remaining differences show up clearly, and we turned them into rules we can test and revise. This italic won’t be the final version, but breaking glyphs in code helps us find the limits faster.

More scripts and Google Fonts

Cyrillic support is planned to match Geist Sans and Geist Mono, and Geist Serif will come to Google Fonts after launch.

One family

With Geist Sans, Geist Mono, Geist Pixel, and now Geist Serif, the family runs from UI text and code to expressive display type, and all four feel at home together.
